title: The four letters, whole
hook: Guru Arjan's longing letters to his father, read in full (Majh M5, ang 96–97)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four watches of the night, and your line: which watch am I in. What did you answer? Today, the week closes with letters a son wrote in the long watches of missing his father. Day six hundred fifty-one.

Early in the path we met young Arjan in Lahore. His father, Guru Ram Das, had sent him there for a family wedding and told him to stay until he was called. Weeks went by. No call came. Arjan wrote home in verse. Tradition says the first two letters never reached his father: his elder brother, Prithi Chand, kept them. So Arjan numbered the third. When Guru Ram Das read a letter marked three, he asked where one and two had gone. Today we read the letters whole, all four stanzas, in order.
screen: `ARJAN, SENT TO LAHORE.` → `TWO LETTERS NEVER ARRIVE.` → `THE THIRD IS NUMBERED.`

segments.voice: They stand in Raag Majh, on angs 96 and 97, as one shabad of four stanzas. The first, in effect: my mind longs for a sight of the Guru. It cries like the chaatrik, the rainbird that tradition says drinks only falling rain. The thirst won't go, no peace comes, without seeing my beloved. And each stanza ends: I am a sacrifice, a sacrifice, to the sight of the Guru. The second: your face is beautiful, your words bring a deep, natural peace. It's been so long since this rainbird saw water. The third, the numbered one, is the sharpest. When I can't meet you for even a moment, it's the dark age for me. When will I meet you, beloved? The night won't pass; sleep won't come. Then the fourth, written after the reunion. Tradition says Guru Ram Das sent for him, and soon named him the fifth Guru. And the last stanza turns: by good fortune I've met the Guru, and found the eternal Lord within my own home. Read whole, the letters have a shape. Longing, then memory, then near despair, then arrival. Sikhs hear two loves in them at once: a son for his father, and a soul for the One. Guru Arjan doesn't separate them. Now, the week. The Ardas closed, a whole people's prayer. Then shabad, a hymn for every moment. Palaces of pearls: may I not forget. Greed is a dog. The river and the fish. The four watches of a life. And the four letters: longing that gets an answer.
screen: `ONE: I CRY LIKE THE RAINBIRD.` · `TWO: SO LONG SINCE I SAW WATER.` · `THREE: A MOMENT AWAY IS A DARK AGE.` · `FOUR: FOUND IN MY OWN HOME.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE LONGING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a letter to someone you miss. Bring them to mind: someone far away, someone you've drifted from, someone who has died. Begin the letter in your head, or on paper if you have it. Start the way Arjan did, with the plain truth: I miss you. Then one thing you remember about them. Then what the missing feels like, honestly. Don't worry about sending it. If you pray, you can hold them before the One with a quiet Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
The four letters. Guru Arjan's four stanzas in Raag Majh: longing like the rainbird, then the third letter's dark night, then the reunion, found in his own home.
Your line: the whole longing. Today, finish the letter you started, and if the person is living and reachable, think about sending it. Day six hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Arjan's Majh shabad 'meraa man lochai gur darsan taaee' in kirtan, and tell the story of the letters from Lahore that led to his being named the fifth Guru.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sight, seeing the beloved; the letters long for the Guru's darshan.

trapdoor: what you thought: homesick letters from a young man.
what it means: one shabad in four stanzas, longing for a father and for the One, ending in reunion.

what a scholar hears: the shabad's arc, from the chaatrik's thirst to 'found within my own home', joins the succession story to a theology of the Lord found within; the letter narrative comes from Sikh tradition.

notes: Paraphrased; confirm the four stanzas as summarized, especially stanza 3 ('ik gharee na milte taa kalijug hotaa') and stanza 4 ('bhaag hoaa gur sant milaaiaa, prabh abinaasee ghar meh paaiaa').
The interception by Prithi Chand and the numbered third letter are traditional, said 'tradition says'.
Y1 day 58 introduced the letters; this day reads all four as the outline asks. Week look-back covers days 645–651.
